deadhead-miles.html.text:
← Owner-operator cost per mile calculator

How deadhead miles cut a loaded rate

Brokers quote dollars per loaded mile. The truck burns diesel on every mile. Those are not the same unit, and treating them as if they were is how a $2.00 offer books and the week still loses money.

Take a common solo week: 1,800 loaded miles and 450 empty miles. That is 2,250 total miles and 20% deadhead. A $2.00 loaded offer produces $3,600 of gross. Spread over every mile the truck moved, that is $1.60 of revenue per mile — before the factor takes 2–4%.

Same week, after 3% factoring. $3,600 × 0.97 = $3,492 settled. $3,492 ÷ 2,250 miles = $1.55 per total mile. If all-in cost is $1.57, the posted $2.00 load is underwater even though it looks like a 40-cent cushion over a $1.60 CPM someone quoted on loaded miles only.

The conversion that keeps the units honest:

  1. Cost the whole week on total miles (fuel, reserves, weekly share of the note).
  2. Divide that weekly cost by loaded miles. That is the break-even loaded rate.
  3. Compare the offer after factoring to that number — not to all-in CPM, and not to last month’s average.

A short week makes this worse. The truck payment and insurance do not shrink when you run 1,600 miles instead of 2,400. Fixed cost per mile goes up, so the loaded rate that covered last week may not cover this one.

Open the calculator and replace the starting week with your own miles and notes. Nothing is uploaded.

No warranty. This page is free arithmetic, not legal, tax, financial, or dispatch advice. Verify every figure before you book a load. The authors accept no liability for loss from its use.

does-detention-pay-cover-the-wait.html.text:
← Owner-operator cost per mile calculator

Does detention pay cover the wait?

Sitting unpaid is not the same as a cheap loaded rate. Detention is a settlement line. A lumper is cash out unless someone reimburses it. Treating both as “part of the $2.00” hides whether the wait actually paid.

On the calculator’s starting week — 1,800 loaded / 450 empty, $2.00 after 3% factoring — the miles-only settlement loses $32.96. That is the hole detention has to fill before the wait is even free.

Six hours at $50, same 3% factor, plus a $75 lumper you paid. Detention settles $291. Subtract the lumper and the accessorials add $216. The same $2.00 week keeps $183.04. The miles-only hole closes after 0.68 hours at that detention rate. Past that, extra hours are profit — until the next load you missed is worth more than sitting.

The conversion that keeps the units honest:

  1. Score the offer on miles and the note only. That is the miles-only profit.
  2. Add detention hours × pay, plus layover, after the same factor if they settle with the load.
  3. Subtract lumper paid minus lumper reimbursed. That is extra weekly cost.

Unpaid detention is just more unpaid time. A lumper the broker never repays is a rate cut you already accepted. Open the calculator and replace the starting hours with the ones on your bills. Nothing is uploaded.

No warranty. This page is free arithmetic, not legal, tax, financial, or dispatch advice. Verify every figure against your own settlement before you sit or drop. The authors accept no liability for loss from its use.

index.html.text:
FOR OWNER-OPERATORS

Price the week, not the loaded mile.

A $2.00 loaded offer is not $2.00 in your pocket. Empty miles still burn diesel and the truck note does not care whether the trailer is full. Enter a week of running — fuel, the note, insurance, deadhead — and see the all-in cost per mile and the loaded rate that actually covers it.

This week’s miles

Count every mile the truck moves. Deadhead, bobtail, and empty repositioning belong in the empty box — they are why a rate that looked fine on the load board does not cover the week.

Fixed cost (monthly)

These do not drop when you sit. A short week makes them more expensive per mile, which is why a rate that worked at 2,400 miles can lose money at 1,800.

Per-mile reserves and the offer

Nothing withholds tax for you. Put in whatever share of profit you set aside for self-employment and income tax and the target below becomes what you actually keep. Leave it at 0 and every figure behaves exactly as before. We do not guess the percentage — it depends on your filing status, state, deductions, and per-diem election, and picking one for you would be a claim about what you owe. Ask your tax preparer for yours.

Detention, layover, and lumper

Miles do not pay you while you sit. Detention and layover are settlement lines; a dock lumper is cash out unless the broker reimburses it. Starting figures: 6 hours at $50, a $75 lumper you paid. Does detention pay cover the wait?

Break-even loaded rate

$—
per loaded mile to cover this week

Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting figures are a typical solo dry-van week, not a benchmark or a recommended rate. Replace them with your fuel receipts and the truck note.

Hauling cars? The car hauler load planner picks which vehicles to carry and on which deck.

What this checks

Generic “cost per mile” pages often divide monthly bills by loaded miles and stop. The decision an owner-operator actually faces is whether this week’s empty miles and this settlement’s factoring still leave the posted rate above cost. How deadhead miles cut a loaded rate walks through that in search-query words. See also: this calculator vs. ATBS, for when to reach for a free instant calculator and when to hire a paid bookkeeping service, and this calculator vs. DAT RateView, for market rate versus your own break-even. And if you already work your cost per mile out yourself, this calculator vs. dividing your bills by your miles shows the four things that division cannot see, in dollars.

It does not tell you which load to book, what a broker should pay, or what your truck is worth. The gap between the posted rate and the break-even loaded rate is arithmetic on the numbers you typed.

Common questions

How do owner operators calculate cost per mile?

Add every mile the truck moves that week — loaded and empty. Divide fuel, per-mile reserves, and the weekly share of the truck note, insurance, and permits by those total miles. That is all-in cost per mile. Then divide the same weekly cost by loaded miles only to get the loaded rate that covers the empty ones.

How does deadhead affect a trucking rate?

Revenue is paid only on loaded miles. Cost is incurred on every mile. A 20% empty week means the loaded rate must cover 25% more cost than the all-in CPM. A $2.00 loaded offer on that week is $1.60 of revenue per total mile before factoring.

Does this calculator use a different fuel mileage for loaded and empty miles?

No — it takes one “Average MPG” figure and divides it into every mile the truck moved that week, loaded and empty combined (fuel gallons = total miles ÷ MPG). It does not model the real gap between loaded and unladen fuel economy. At the starting figures — 2,250 total miles at 6.2 MPG, $4.20 diesel — that is $1,524.19 of fuel for the week, regardless of how the 1,800 loaded and 450 empty miles split it. If your logbook shows loaded and empty MPG separately, enter the mileage weighted for the week’s actual mix (total gallons actually burned ÷ total miles run), not your best-case unladen number, or the fuel line will understate cost on a week with a lot of loaded miles.

What loaded rate should I accept?

This page does not tell you what to accept. It reports the loaded rate that covers the costs you entered, after deadhead and after any factoring percent you set. Compare an offer to that number. Verify every figure against your own fuel receipts and notes before you book a load.

How much does factoring actually cost on a load?

Factoring takes its percent off gross revenue before the money settles, not off profit. On the starting figures — 1,800 loaded miles at a $2.00 offer, $3,600 gross — 3% factoring is a $108 fee, leaving $3,492 net from the miles. The offered rate itself doesn’t change; the calculator’s “effective loaded rate” ($1.94/mi at those figures) is what you actually settle for, and that’s the number to compare against break-even, not the rate on the rate confirmation.

Does an unreimbursed lumper fee change the cost per mile?

No — it’s added to the week’s cost as a flat dollar amount, not spread across miles. “Lumper you paid” minus “Lumper reimbursed” becomes a straight addition to weekly cost regardless of how many miles were run that week. At the starting figures, a $75 lumper the broker never reimburses is $75 straight off the week, on top of fuel, reserves, and fixed cost.

How much does a short week raise cost per mile?

Fixed costs — the truck note, insurance, permits — are billed monthly and this calculator converts them to a weekly figure by dividing by 52÷12 weeks, then spreads that over total miles run. Fewer miles in the week means the same dollar figure divides over less distance. At the starting figures ($5,550/month fixed, about $1,281/week) run over 2,250 total miles, fixed cost alone is about $0.57/mi; the same $1,281 spread over a 1,500-mile week would be about $0.85/mi — the truck note doesn’t get cheaper because the week was slow.

How many loaded miles does it take to break even at an offered rate?

“Loaded miles to cover this week at offer” divides the week’s cost, minus any detention/layover that’s already been factored in, by the settled effective rate — the offered rate after factoring. At the starting figures, a $2.00/mi offer settles to $1.94/mi after 3% factoring, and it takes roughly 1,706 loaded miles against the week’s cost (after the $291 of factored accessorials) to break even. The starting 1,800 loaded miles clears that, leaving around $183 for the week.

What loaded rate do I need to hit a weekly take-home goal?

Type a dollar figure into “Target weekly take-home” and the calculator solves the loaded rate backwards instead of forwards: take the week’s cost, subtract the detention/layover income already counted, add the take-home you want, divide by loaded miles, then gross that up for the cut factoring will take. At the starting figures — $3,600 weekly cost, $291 of factored accessorial income, 1,800 loaded miles, 3% factoring — an $800 take-home goal solves to about $2.35/mi loaded, before factoring. That’s the number to compare against a broker’s posted rate, not the $2.00 starting example; the $2.00 offer only clears about $183 for the week at these figures.

Running several stops a day? The route stop optimizer finds the order that cuts drive time and shows the miles and dollars saved.

Driving a personal vehicle for a delivery or rideshare app instead? The gig driver net pay calculator turns one session’s gross app pay into net pay per hour and per mile after gas and vehicle wear — nothing uploaded.

Choosing among several loads this week? The owner operator load chain planner finds the best chain from your shortlist, with the empty run, the wait for pickup windows and rest priced in, and the lowest rate each load is worth — nothing uploaded.

Running scheduled or STAT medical courier routes instead of long-haul freight? The medical courier route margin calculator prices paid wait, deadhead, loaded labor, and temperature-control consumables per route.

Waited at a dock longer than the free time? The truck detention pay calculator turns your gate times into the detention you are owed and a claim email for the broker — nothing uploaded.

Filing Form 2290 for the truck? The Form 2290 heavy vehicle use tax calculator prices each truck by weight category and first-use month and shows when it is due — nothing uploaded.

The “permits, plates, IFTA, ELD” line above is a monthly average; the quarterly return behind it is its own piece of arithmetic. The IFTA quarterly fuel tax calculator works the jurisdiction schedule from your miles and gallons — including the Indiana, Kentucky and Virginia surcharge, which is charged on every taxable gallon you burned there and is never reduced by fuel you bought there.

vs-atbs.html.text:
← Owner Operator CPM Calculator

This calculator vs. ATBS

ATBS (American Truck Business Services) is a well-known tax, bookkeeping, and business-support company built for owner-operators, with tiered service plans (RumbleStrip Essentials, Professional, and Enterprise) described on atbs.com/pricing. It is a paid, ongoing service — you sign up as a client and they handle recurring bookkeeping, tax prep, and business reporting for your trucking business over time.

That makes it the right choice for one job: outsourcing the ongoing bookkeeping, quarterly taxes, and year-round business paperwork that come with running a truck. This page does not do that job, and does not try to. It has no accounts, keeps no records between visits, and files nothing with anyone.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Should I book this load, right now, at this posted rate? This calculator — enter this week's miles, fuel, and fixed costs, get a break-even loaded rate in seconds, no signup.
What are my quarterly estimated taxes, and is my bookkeeping in order for the IRS? ATBS or another paid bookkeeping/tax service — that is ongoing professional work this page does not do.
What was my actual cost per mile last month, reconciled against real invoices and receipts? ATBS, or your own records — this calculator only computes forward from the numbers you type in for one week; it stores nothing and reconciles nothing.
Does an empty-mile-heavy week and factoring still leave a posted rate profitable? This calculator — the deadhead-adjusted break-even rate and factoring math are built for exactly that question.

This calculator is deliberately the opposite shape from a bookkeeping service: it has no account to create, remembers nothing about you between visits, and never uploads a number you type. That makes it useful for the in-the-moment question — does this load cover this week — and useless for the longer-term job a paid service like ATBS is built to do: keeping a real, reconciled set of books over a year.

It needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or hire ATBS?

They answer different questions. ATBS is a paid, ongoing tax, bookkeeping, and business-support service built for owner-operators — you become a client and they handle recurring accounting work over time. This page is a free, instant calculator: type in one week's miles, fuel, truck note, and insurance, and see the all-in cost per mile and the break-even loaded rate for that week, right now, with no signup and no ongoing relationship. Many owner-operators use a free calculator like this one to sanity-check a load offer in the moment, and a paid service like ATBS for taxes, quarterly tax estimates, and year-round bookkeeping — the two are not substitutes for each other.

Is this page affiliated with ATBS?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by ATBS (American Truck Business Services) or RumbleStrip. ATBS and RumbleStrip are named here only to describe what this calculator is for, based on ATBS's own public pricing page.

Open the Owner Operator Cost Per Mile Calculator to run this week's numbers.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, financial, or business advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. Verify every figure against your own fuel receipts, insurance, and notes before relying on it or booking a load.

vs-dat-rateview.html.text:
← Owner Operator CPM Calculator

This calculator vs. DAT RateView

DAT RateView, part of DAT iQ from DAT Freight & Analytics, is a paid subscription tool that reports average spot and contract freight rates per lane, drawn from a large database of real freight invoices and transactions rather than posted bids, with day, week, and multi-month history. It answers a market question: what has this lane been paying, across many carriers, lately.

That makes it the right tool for one job: checking whether a posted rate is competitive against what the market has actually been paying on this lane. This page does not do that job, and does not try to. It has no rate database, no lane history, and no idea what any other carrier got paid this week — it only knows what you type in about this truck.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Does this offer cover my fuel, truck note, insurance, and this week's deadhead? This calculator — enter this week's miles, fuel, and fixed costs, get a break-even loaded rate in seconds, no signup.
Is this offer high, low, or average for what this lane has been paying lately? DAT RateView or a similar market-rate tool — that reads real transaction data across many carriers, which this page never collects or sees.
What did this lane pay last week, or over the last 90 days? DAT RateView's own history — this calculator keeps no history between visits and stores nothing about past weeks or past loads.
Does a deadhead-heavy week and factoring still leave a posted rate above my own cost? This calculator — the deadhead-adjusted break-even rate and factoring math are built for exactly that question, and a market-average tool does not know your deadhead at all.

The two are not substitutes, and using only one leaves a real gap. A load that DAT RateView shows as paying at or above the lane average can still be a losing week if the deadhead getting into position is long, the truck note is high, or the diesel price ran up. A load that shows below the lane average can still clear this truck's break-even easily on a short, efficient week. Market position and personal break-even are answers to different questions, and a rate can pass one test and fail the other in either direction.

This calculator needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. It has no lane database because it is not trying to be one.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or DAT RateView?

They answer different questions. DAT RateView is a paid subscription product from DAT Freight & Analytics that reports average spot and contract rates per lane, built from a large database of real freight invoices and transactions with day-by-day and multi-month history. It tells you what a lane has been paying across the market. This page is a free, instant calculator: type in one week's miles, fuel, truck note, and insurance, and see the all-in cost per mile and the break-even loaded rate for that week, right now, with no signup. It has no market data at all and does not know what other carriers are getting paid on this lane — it only knows what this truck costs to run. A rate can be at or above the market average DAT reports and still lose money on a deadhead-heavy week, and a rate can be below the market average and still clear this truck's cost on a short, efficient one. Checking market position and checking your own break-even are two separate questions, and neither answers the other.

Is this page affiliated with DAT RateView?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by DAT Freight & Analytics or DAT RateView. DAT and DAT RateView are trademarks of their owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not, based on DAT's own public description of the RateView product.

vs-dividing-your-bills-by-your-miles.htm.text:
← Owner-Operator Cost Per Mile Calculator

This calculator vs. dividing your bills by your miles

Add up the month’s bills, divide by the miles you ran, call that your cost per mile. It is the arithmetic every owner-operator already knows, it is not wrong, and if you take it off your own settlement statements it is better cost data than anything you can type into a web page. It also answers a different question from the one a broker is asking you.

Cost rides on every mile. Revenue only rides on the loaded ones.

That one sentence is the whole difference. The division gives you cost per total mile. The number you quote, accept or turn down is a loaded rate. They are not the same figure and the gap is the size of your deadhead.

Here is an illustrative week — your numbers will differ, and these are not a claim about what anything costs. 2,000 loaded miles and 500 empty, so 2,500 total and 20% deadhead. 6.5 mpg at $3.90 a gallon. Monthly fixed of $4,100 (truck payment $2,200, insurance $1,100, permits $200, other $600). Reserves of 25¢ a mile for maintenance, tires and the rest.

FigureThis weekWhat it is
Weekly cost, all in$3,071.15Fuel, reserves, and the monthly fixed bills spread over the week.
Bills ÷ miles$1.23Cost per total mile. Correct, and not the rate you quote.
Break-even loaded rate$1.54Cost per loaded mile — the same cost, carried by the 2,000 miles that actually earn.
A $1.65 offer looks like42¢…of margin, measured against the first figure.
A $1.65 offer really is11¢…of margin, measured against the rate you are actually being offered.

The relationship is exact rather than a rule of thumb: the break-even loaded rate is the all-in cost per total mile divided by one minus the empty share. At 20% deadhead that is a 25% markup on the divided figure, every week, in the direction that makes a thin load look fat.

Each figure in the table is produced by the same calculateWeek the calculator runs, from the inputs listed above, and a test in this venture recomputes them and fails if the page and the model ever disagree.

Three more things the division cannot see

1. A short week raises your cost per mile without a single bill changing

This is the one that hides best, because a cost per mile worked out once looks like a property of the truck. It is not; it is a property of the week. The truck payment, the insurance and the permits do not care how far you went, so the fewer miles you turn, the more of them each mile carries.

Same bills as above, but a 1,500-mile week instead of a 2,500-mile one (1,200 loaded, 300 empty, the same 20% empty share):

Figure2,500-mile week1,500-mile week
Fixed cost per mile$0.38$0.63
All-in cost per total mile$1.23$1.48
Break-even loaded rate$1.54$1.85

A rate you could take all day in the first week loses money in the second, and nothing about your costs changed. Quoting a single remembered cost per mile through a slow month is how that happens without anyone noticing.

2. Factoring is charged on revenue, so it is not in the pile you divided

There is no invoice for it to arrive on. It comes off the top of what the broker pays, which means a bills-divided-by-miles figure cannot contain it by construction — and it is not small. In the 2,500-mile week, taking that $1.65 with a 3% factoring fee:

FigureNo factoring3% factoring
Effective loaded rate$1.65$1.60
Week’s profit$228.85$129.85

Five cents a mile off the rate, and 43% of the profit off the week. Whether you factor is a cash-flow decision with good reasons on both sides; what it is not is invisible.

3. A lumper you paid and did not get back lands on the load, not on an average

Per-mile thinking wants to smear it across the year. The money left this week. A $150 lumper you were not reimbursed for raises the break-even loaded rate on that 2,000-loaded-mile week from $1.54 to $1.61 — seven cents, on one receipt. Detention and layover work the same way in reverse, and the calculator will tell you whether the detention being offered actually covers the hours you are being asked to sit.

What dividing your bills by your miles does better

The honest half, and it matters more than it usually gets said. Where this page and your own arithmetic disagree about what your costs are, your arithmetic wins:

  • It is a measurement; this page is an estimate. Your settlement statements, fuel receipts and repair invoices are what actually happened to your truck. Every number on this page is one you typed, and it has no way to check a single one of them.
  • It catches costs you would forget to enter. A division over a full year sweeps up the annual permit, the DOT physical, the tyre you bought in cash, the week the APU died. A form asks only what it thought to ask.
  • Averaged over a long enough period, it is the better cost base. A single week is noisy. If you have twelve months of statements, the cost per mile they give you is a sounder input to this page than the figures you would guess — so bring it here rather than replacing it.

So these are sequential, not competing. Work your real costs out from your own statements; then use this page to turn them into the loaded rate you can accept this week, with the empty miles, the short week, the factoring fee and the unreimbursed lumper each put where they land instead of averaged into one number that is right about last year and silent about the load in front of you.

No account, no sign-in, nothing uploaded: the arithmetic runs in your browser and the page keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

What is wrong with dividing my monthly bills by my miles?

Nothing, as arithmetic — it gives you a true cost per total mile, and if you take it off your own settlement statements over a full year it is more trustworthy than anything you can type into a calculator. The problem is that it answers a different question from the one you ask at the load board. Cost lands on every mile you turn, loaded or empty. Revenue lands only on loaded miles. So the number you need when a broker names a rate is cost divided by loaded miles, and the division most people run divides by total miles instead. On a week that is 20% empty, that is a 31 cent per mile gap in the illustrative week on this page — and it is a gap in the direction that makes a losing load look profitable.

How much does deadhead actually change my break-even rate?

By the deadhead share, compounding. The relationship is exact: break-even loaded rate equals all-in cost per total mile divided by (1 minus the empty share). In the week worked through on this page — 2,000 loaded miles and 500 empty, so 20% deadhead — a weekly cost of $3,071.15 is $1.23 per total mile and $1.54 per loaded mile. A broker offering $1.65 looks like 42 cents of margin against the first figure and is really 11 cents against the second. Both numbers are correct arithmetic on the same week; only one of them is the rate you are being asked to accept.

Does a short week really change my cost per mile?

Sharply, and this is the part a single divided figure hides worst, because it looks like a constant. Your truck payment, insurance and permits do not care how many miles you ran, so the fewer you turn the more of them each mile has to carry. Same bills as the illustrative week above, but 1,200 loaded and 300 empty instead of 2,000 and 500: fixed cost per mile goes from 38 cents to 63 cents, and the break-even loaded rate from $1.54 to $1.85. Nothing changed but the miles. A cost per mile worked out on a good month and then quoted from all year is wrong on every week that is not that month.

Why does factoring not show up in my cost per mile?

Because it is charged on revenue, not on cost, so it is not in the pile of bills you are dividing — there is no invoice for it to appear on. It still comes straight off the rate the broker quoted. In the illustrative week, a 3% factoring fee turns an accepted $1.65 into an effective $1.60 per loaded mile, and the week's profit from $228.85 to $129.85. That is 43% of the profit, on a cost line that a bills-divided-by-miles figure cannot contain by construction.

Should I stop working out my cost per mile from my own statements?

No — keep doing it, and trust it over this page where the two disagree about what your costs are. Your settlement statements and fuel receipts are measurements of your actual truck; every figure on this page is one you typed, and it has no way to check any of them. What it adds is not better cost data. It is the step after: taking the costs you already know and turning them into the loaded rate you can accept this week, with the empty miles, the short week, the factoring fee and the unreimbursed lumper each put where they actually land instead of averaged into one number.

Run your own week in the cost per mile calculator, or read the worked examples on how deadhead miles cut a loaded rate and whether detention pay covers the wait.

Illustrative figures only. Every dollar amount on this page comes from one made-up week, chosen to show the size of an effect. It is not a claim about what fuel, insurance, factoring, lumpers or freight cost, and nothing here is a rate you should quote. Put your own numbers in the calculator.
